usage: 여보세요?
Hello?
Rising intonation when you pick up an unknown call; the tone alone signals you're waiting for the caller to speak
여보세요, 안녕하세요.
Hello, hi there.
여보세요 opens the voice channel, then 안녕하세요 is the actual social greeting — both are normally said in quick succession
여보세요, 들리세요?
Hello, can you hear me?
Re-used mid-call to check a silent line; the attention-getting origin makes it natural as a line-test signal
여보세요, 거기 한국식당이죠?
Hello, is that the Korean restaurant?
Confirming you reached the right place after dialling; 이죠? seeks confirmation with a soft rising tone
examples: A: 여보세요? / B: 네, 여보세요. 어떻게 도와드릴까요?
A: Hello? / B: Yes, hello. How can I help you?
Classic call-centre exchange showing 여보세요 as both the caller's opener and the agent's polite response; the agent pairs it with a service phrase
여보세요, 김민수 씨 휴대폰 맞으세요?
Hello, is this Kim Minsu's phone?
Number-check right after the opener — notice 맞으세요? ('is this correct?') rather than the blunt '누구세요?'
여보세요? 여보세요? 소리가 자꾸 끊겨요.
Hello? Hello? It keeps cutting out.
Repeated on a dropping line; the doubling is natural Korean stress, not impatience
nuance: 여보세요 is Korean's dedicated telephone 'hello' and almost never appears face to face — the rare exception is snapping a daydreamer to attention, where it works like English 'hello? anybody home?' The phrase evolved from 여기 보세요 ('look/attend over here'), a call for attention, which also explains why it works mid-call when a line goes suspiciously quiet. Crucially, it is NOT a wellbeing greeting: 안녕하세요 asks 'are you at peace?' and is the true in-person or opening-the-conversation greeting; 여보세요 merely opens the voice channel. Register is neutral-polite thanks to the -세요 ending, appropriate for strangers, customer service, and elders alike, but never truncated to 여보 — that independent word has drifted to mean 'honey/darling' between spouses. The English-speaker trap is treating it like a general 'hi', using it to greet someone face to face or at the start of a KakaoTalk voice note; keep it firmly in the phone or attention-getting lane.

structuredNuance.t: 여보세요 evolved from 여기 보세요 ('look/attend here') — a literal call for attention. Its real function today is simply opening a telephone voice channel; it carries no social warmth the way 안녕하세요 does. Think of it as 'channel open' not 'nice to meet you'.

Use it the moment you answer or place a call — with strangers, customer service, elders, or close friends alike. The -세요 ending keeps it comfortably polite across all relationships. On a bad line it doubles naturally (여보세요? 여보세요?) without sounding rude. Face to face it works only for theatrical effect ('hello? are you listening?').

안녕하세요 is the in-person social greeting ('are you at peace?'); 여보세요 is only a call-opener. They are not interchangeable: starting a phone call with 안녕하세요 alone sounds like you skipped the channel-open step, and saying 여보세요 to someone standing next to you sounds like a joke.

여보세요 has no register upgrade — you cannot make it more formal by adding particles or endings. The only contraction is 여보, which applies exclusively to a spouse (배우자에게만) and carries the meaning 'honey/darling'. In practice, phone callers immediately follow 여보세요 with either 안녕하세요 to add social warmth, or 저는 OO입니다 to introduce themselves. On business calls 여보세요, 안녕하세요, 저 ○○회사 ○○○입니다 is the full three-step opener.

English speakers often use 여보세요 as a general 'hi' when meeting someone, or drop it into a KakaoTalk voice note opener. Both are wrong. Also: shortening to 여보 with a stranger signals 'darling' — keep the full form.

mistakes: Using 여보세요 to greet someone in person — it only belongs on the phone or to snap a distracted person back; for meeting people say 안녕하세요.
Shortening it to 여보 to sound casual — 여보 alone means 'dear/honey' between spouses, so to a stranger it's bizarre; always keep the full 여보세요.
Treating it as a complete greeting and saying nothing else on a polite call — after 여보세요 you still add 안녕하세요 or state who you are, because 여보세요 only opens the channel.

usage: 누구세요?
Who is it?
Standard polite 'who's calling' on an unknown number — the question stands alone with a slight rising tone
실례지만 누구세요?
Excuse me, who is this?
실례지만 ('pardon the rudeness, but') softens a direct identity question to near-formality level
전화 누구셨어요?
Who was that on the phone?
Past tense, asking a family member after they've hung up — 셨어요 is the honorific past
혹시 누구세요?
Might I ask who this is?
혹시 ('by any chance') makes the question maximally tentative and polite, good when you want to be very gentle
examples: A: 여보세요, 박 사장님 계십니까? / B: 누구세요?
A: Hello, is President Park available? / B: Who's calling?
Reception gatekeeping: the receptionist asks identity before deciding whether to connect — note 계십니까 (formal) in the request
죄송하지만 누구세요? 성함을 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?
Sorry, who is this? Could you say your name again?
Polite follow-up when a name was unclear — 말씀해 주시겠어요 is deferential, suitable for an important caller
A: 여보세요. / B: 안녕하세요, 실례지만 누구세요?
A: Hello. / B: Hi there — excuse me, who is this?
Shows 실례지만 cushioning the question in an everyday answer-the-phone scenario
nuance: 누구세요? is the polite identity question built from 누구 ('who') and the honorific copula -(이)세요, so it paradoxically honors the stranger whose identity you don't yet know. That politeness is essential: drop to 누구야? or 누구냐? and you sound suspicious or confrontational, fine only with close friends. In formal business settings Koreans upgrade further to 누구시죠? (ever so slightly more formal) or replace the whole question with 어디세요? — literally 'where are you from?', idiomatically asking which company or department. A grammar trap: no particle goes between 누구 and 세요 — 누구가세요 is ungrammatical. The social trap is using 누구세요? on a call YOU placed: if you dialled someone, you introduce yourself first (저 민수예요) and never begin by demanding the other person identify themselves — that inversion is rude. Soft lead-ins like 실례지만 or 혹시 are expected in professional situations to keep the question from sounding like an interrogation.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'who (honorific) are you?' — but the real job is a polite identity check on an incoming call. The honorific -세요 embedded in the question signals that you are treating this stranger respectfully even as you ask them to identify themselves.

Use only when you RECEIVE a call from an unknown number. On a business call, pair with 실례지만 or 혹시 to soften it. To a caller from an important company, upgrade to 어디세요? ('which organization are you calling from?') — the standard in formal Korean office settings. Never use it when you placed the call; introduce yourself instead.

누구야? / 누구냐? are 반말 and sound suspicious or hostile to a stranger — use only with close friends. 어디세요? is the formal business replacement that asks 'which organization?' rather than just 'who?', softer and more professionally appropriate when the caller is likely a client or official.

The register ladder runs: 누구야? (반말, close friends only) → 누구세요? (neutral-polite, the everyday default) → 누구시죠? (slightly more formal; -시죠 is more deferential than -세요) → 어디세요? (formal business; shifts from personal identity to organizational affiliation). Add 실례지만 or 혹시 at any level to soften. In writing or formal announcements you may see 성함이 어떻게 되세요? ('may I ask your name?') as an even gentler alternative.

Do not add a subject particle — 누구가세요 / 누구이세요 is ungrammatical. And never ask 누구세요? on a call you made — you introduce yourself first; the question is reserved for the person answering an unexpected call.

mistakes: Saying 누구야? or 누구냐? to a stranger — these are 반말 and sound like a challenge or suspicion; the honorific 누구세요? is required with anyone you don't know.
Adding a subject particle: 누구가세요 / 누구이세요 is wrong — the question is simply 누구 + 세요, with no 가/이 between them.
Using 누구세요? on a call you yourself placed — the caller identifies themselves first (저 민수예요); 누구세요? is only for the person who answers an unknown incoming call.

usage: 지금 통화 괜찮아요?
Is now okay to talk?
지금 ('now') pins the question to this exact moment — the most common opening line after 여보세요
잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?
Got a minute to talk?
잠깐 signals you plan to be brief — a considerate way to set expectations before you start
통화 괜찮으세요?
Is it all right to talk?
괜찮으세요 lifts the register to deferential — use with clients, customers, or elders
나중에 통화 괜찮아요?
Would later be okay to talk?
Offering a callback if this moment is inconvenient — note it switches from a present check to a future offer
examples: A: 여보세요, 지금 통화 괜찮아요? / B: 잠깐만요, 회의 중이라서요. 이따가 다시 걸어도 될까요?
A: Hello, is now a good time to talk? / B: One sec — I'm in a meeting. Can I call you back later?
Classic real-world exchange: one person checks timing, the other declines politely and suggests a callback — very natural and complete
혹시 바쁘세요? 잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?
Are you busy by any chance? Got a moment to talk?
혹시 softens the question further — useful when you're unsure about the other person's schedule
지금 통화 괜찮으세요? 업무 관련해서 여쭤볼 게 있어서요.
Is now convenient to talk? I have a work-related question.
Upgrading to 괜찮으세요 for a professional context and giving a reason up front — reduces the chance they decline
nuance: 통화 괜찮아요? is the standard Korean 'is now a good time to talk?' and it hinges on a word distinction English smooths over: 통화 (通話) is the actual connected voice conversation, while 전화 (電話) is the phone device or the act of calling. Asking 전화 괜찮아요? would mean 'is the phone okay?' — odd — because you want to ask about the act of conversing, not the hardware. 괜찮아요 ('it's fine / no problem') here means 'is it convenient'. The closest near-synonym 시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?') is broader — it works for in-person meetings too — whereas 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically 'can we talk right now on this line'. Register: the 요-ending is polite-casual, right for friends and colleagues; bump to 통화 괜찮으세요? for clients or elders, or add a reason (업무 관련이라서요) to pre-justify the call. English speakers often try 말할 수 있어요? ('can you speak?'), which tests physical ability rather than availability — awkward and clinical; the natural frame is always the convenience check.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'is the phone-call okay?' — but the real meaning is 'is this a convenient moment for you to talk?' 괜찮아요 shifts from its base meaning 'fine/no problem' to a convenience check the moment it is combined with a situational noun like 통화.

Say it right after 여보세요 — it is the polite opener for every unplanned call. The 요-form is standard with friends, coworkers, and acquaintances. For clients or seniors, use 통화 괜찮으세요? or the fuller 지금 잠깐 통화 가능하세요? Tip: adding 잠깐 ('briefly') signals you won't take long and reduces the chance they decline.

시간 괜찮아요? ('do you have time?') is broader — it applies to both calls and in-person meetings. 통화 괜찮아요? is specifically for right now on the phone. Neither should be replaced with 전화 괜찮아요? — that asks about the device/act of calling, not the conversation itself.

The register ladder runs: 지금 통화 괜찮아요? (casual-polite, everyday default) → 통화 괜찮으세요? (one step up; the -으세요 suffix adds deference, used with clients or seniors) → 지금 잠깐 통화 가능하세요? (more formal; 가능하다 'possible' is colder but clearer) → 통화 가능한 시간 알려 주시겠어요? (fully formal written-level; asks them to name a convenient time slot). Add 잠깐 to any form to imply brevity and reduce hesitation.

Translating 'can you talk?' as 말할 수 있어요? asks about physical ability and sounds clinical — the Korean way is the convenience check 통화 괜찮아요? Also, swapping in 전화 is wrong: 전화 괜찮아요? asks if the phone itself is okay, not if the moment is convenient.

mistakes: Saying 말할 수 있어요? for 'can you talk?' — that tests physical speaking ability; the natural phone courtesy check is 통화 괜찮아요?
Swapping in 전화 to get 전화 괜찮아요? — 전화 (電話) is the device or the act of phoning; the ongoing voice conversation is 통화 (通話), so always use 통화 for this question.
Dropping the courtesy check entirely and launching straight into your business — Koreans almost always open with 통화 괜찮아요? to respect the other person's time, especially on an unplanned call.

usage: 잘 안 들려요.
I can't hear you well.
잘 = 'well'; 안 = negation; 들리다 = passive 'to be audible' — the sound isn't reaching the ear
소리가 잘 안 들려요.
The sound isn't coming through.
소리가 as the grammatical subject makes clear it's the sound that's failing, not your listening effort
뚝뚝 끊겨서 잘 안 들려요.
It's choppy so I can't hear.
뚝뚝 끊기다 = the onomatopoeic phrase for a breaking-up line — very natural and native-sounding
조금만 크게 말씀해 주세요, 잘 안 들려요.
Could you speak a bit louder? I can't hear well.
크게 말씀해 주세요 = polite request for more volume; note 말씀 as the honorific form of 말
examples: A: 여보세요? 잘 안 들려요. / B: 저도요. 지금 신호가 약한 것 같아요.
A: Hello? I can't hear you well. / B: Same here. I think the signal is weak right now.
Both sides confirming a bad line — 저도요 ('me too') and 신호가 약하다 are the most natural collocations for this situation
목소리가 잘 안 들려요. 좀 크게 말해 줄 수 있어요?
I can't hear your voice well. Can you speak up a bit?
목소리가 as the subject clarifies the problem is volume, not connection — good when the line is clear but the person speaks softly
지금 지하철 안이라서 잘 안 들려요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
I'm on the subway so I can't hear well. I'll call back later.
Explaining the cause and offering a callback — 지하철 안 (inside a subway car) is one of the most common real-life reasons
nuance: 잘 안 들려요 rests on a grammatical distinction that trips up every English speaker: 들리다 is the INTRANSITIVE/potential 'to be audible, to be heard' — the sound reaching the ear passively — while 듣다 is the ACTIVE 'to listen'. So a bad line is 안 들려요 ('[your voice] isn't getting through to me'), never 안 들어요, which means 'I am not listening' — implying you're deliberately ignoring them, rude on a call. The vowel contraction is: 들리+어요 → 들려요. Add 잘 ('well') and 안 (negation) for 잘 안 들려요 = 'isn't audibly reaching me well'. For tense: 잘 안 들려요 is ongoing ('I can't hear you'), whereas 잘 안 들렸어요 is past ('I didn't catch that'). Natural subjects to put in front are 소리가 ('the sound'), 목소리가 ('your voice'), or 신호가 약하다 ('the signal is weak'). Register: keep the 요 ending with strangers; dropping to 안 들려 with someone you should address politely is disrespectful.

structuredNuance.t: 'Well not audible-is' — the literal stack of 잘 + 안 + 들리다. The real meaning is 'the sound isn't reaching me clearly'; the SUBJECT is the sound (소리가), not the listener. This passive framing is crucial: the problem is the transmission, not your attention.

Say it the instant the line degrades — with friends, strangers, or clients alike. The 요-form works everywhere. In an office call to a senior, you can be more deferential: 말씀이 잘 안 들려서요, 조금만 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요? If you're the one speaking softly, the other party will tell you 잘 안 들려요 as a signal to raise your voice.

뚝뚝 끊겨요 ('it keeps cutting out') is the standard near-synonym when the problem is a choppy connection rather than low volume. 잘 안 들려요 covers both causes — whether the line breaks up or the other person speaks softly — making it the more versatile phrase. When you want to be specific, say 소리가 잘 안 들려요 for volume and 뚝뚝 끊겨서 잘 안 들려요 for a breaking line.

The core phrase builds outward: 잘 안 들려요 (bare, present — 'I can't hear you') → 잘 안 들렸어요 (past — 'I didn't catch that') → 소리가 잘 안 들려요 (subject added; clarifies the sound is the problem) → 뚝뚝 끊겨서 잘 안 들려요 (onomatopoeic cause; most vivid and native-sounding for a choppy line) → 말씀이 잘 안 들려서요, 조금만 크게 말씀해 주시겠어요? (full deferential form with volume request, best for a senior or client).
Never use 안 들어요 for a bad line — that is the active form and means 'I'm not listening', implying you're ignoring the caller. The passive 들리다 → 안 들려요 is the ONLY correct form for 'can't hear you'.

mistakes: Saying 안 들어요 instead of 안 들려요 — 안 들어요 means 'I'm not listening' (active, rude); the passive potential form 들리다 → 안 들려요 is the only correct choice for a bad connection.
Marking yourself as subject: 저는 안 들려요 sounds awkward — the SOUND is what fails, so either put 소리가 as subject or use the bare 잘 안 들려요.
Clipping to 안 들려 with someone you should be polite to — keep the 요 ending: 잘 안 들려요.

usage: 다시 걸게요.
I'll call back.
걸다 = to place a call (literally 'hook'); 다시 = again — the most concise form
이따 다시 걸게요.
I'll call back in a bit.
이따 = 'a little later today' — signals it won't be long before you redial
제가 다시 걸게요.
I'll be the one to call back.
제가 stresses that YOU will redial — often used to tell the other person not to bother calling again
끊고 다시 걸게요.
Let me hang up and call again.
끊고 links two actions — the fix for a glitchy connection where a fresh call often restores quality
examples: A: 지금 통화 괜찮아요? / B: 미안해요, 지금 회의 중이라서요. 이따 다시 걸게요.
A: Can you talk now? / B: Sorry, I'm in a meeting right now. I'll call back later.
Realistic turn-based exchange: someone checks timing, the other person declines politely and promises a callback with 다시 걸게요
소리가 자꾸 끊겨요. 끊고 다시 걸게요.
It keeps cutting out. I'll hang up and redial.
끊고 daisy-chains the two actions and is the natural Korean fix for choppy audio — 자꾸 ('keeps doing') emphasises the repeated breaks
회의 끝나고 30분 후에 다시 걸게요.
I'll call back 30 minutes after the meeting.
Giving a concrete time is the considerate move — it sets an expectation so the other person doesn't wonder when to expect you
nuance: 다시 걸게요 rests on two points English speakers often miss. First, the verb: Korean 'to place a phone call' is 전화를 걸다 — 걸다 literally 'to hang/hook', a relic of the hook-and-cradle phone era — so you 'hook' a call, and 다시 걸다 = 'hook/call again'. Never use 부르다 ('to call out a name / summon'), which cannot mean telephoning. Second, the ending -ㄹ게요 (걸+게요) is a first-person PROMISE or INTENTION that implies your action is done for the other person's sake: 다시 걸게요 = 'I'll redial, you can count on me'. This is warmer than the neutral future 다시 걸 거예요 ('I will call again' — a mere prediction). Because -ㄹ게요 is first-person only, you cannot say 그 사람이 다시 걸게요 to mean 'he will call'; use 걸 거예요 or 건대요 for third parties. The natural opposite — when THEY should call you — is 다시 걸어 주세요. For clients or formal situations, step up to 다시 연락드리겠습니다 ('I will contact you again', humble and deferential).

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'again hook-will' — 걸다 (to hook/place a call) + 다시 (again). The real meaning is a personal promise to redial, with a connotation of doing so for the listener's benefit. The word 걸다 comes from hooking an old telephone cradle, but today it simply means 'place a call'.

Use on any unplanned call when you need to bow out and ring back — with friends, colleagues, or acquaintances. For a client or senior, upgrade to 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (humble deferential). Pair with 이따 / 나중에 / 끊고 or a specific time to make the promise concrete.

structuredNuance.e: VS 다시 걸 거예요 / 다시 걸어 주세요
structuredNuance.t: 다시 걸 거예요 is a plain future prediction (no personal commitment). 다시 걸게요 is a first-person promise that implies care for the listener — it feels warmer and more reassuring. 다시 걸어 주세요 flips the direction: you are asking THEM to call back.

Register runs: 다시 걸게 (반말 promise, close friends) → 다시 걸게요 (polite promise, everyday default) → 다시 연락드리겠습니다 (humble-formal; 드리겠습니다 replaces the casual ending for clients or seniors). Direction flips: 다시 걸어 주세요 (asking THEM to call back). Timing can be added to any form: 이따 다시 걸게요, 이따 5시에 다시 걸게요. Remember -ㄹ게요 is first-person only — for third parties use 다시 걸 거예요 or 다시 건다고 해요.
Using 부르다 for phoning (다시 불러요) is wrong — 부르다 means calling someone's name or summoning them. Also: saying 다시 걸게요 when the OTHER person should redial — -ㄹ게요 promises YOUR action, not someone else's.

mistakes: Using 부르다 for phoning (다시 불러요) — 부르다 is calling out a name or summoning; a phone call is 전화를 걸다, so 'call back' is 다시 걸게요.
Saying 다시 걸게요 when you want the OTHER person to redial — -ㄹ게요 commits the first-person speaker; if they should call, say 다시 걸어 주세요.
Confusing 다시 걸게요 with the flat prediction 다시 걸 거예요 — the -ㄹ게요 ending makes it a personal promise to the listener, not just a neutral forecast.

usage: 문자 보낼게요.
I'll text you.
문자(를) 보내다 = to send a text message — 를 is often dropped in casual speech
주소 문자로 보낼게요.
I'll send the address by text.
문자로 = 'via text / by text'; 로 marks the means of sending — don't omit this particle
이따 문자 보낼게요.
I'll text in a bit.
이따 sets a soon-ish future time — the most common timing adverb with this phrase
확인하고 문자 보낼게요.
I'll check first and then text you.
Promising a follow-up after doing something — -하고 chains the check with the send
examples: A: 장소가 어디예요? / B: 지금 전화하기 어렵네요. 문자 보낼게요.
A: Where's the venue? / B: It's hard to talk right now. I'll text you.
Real exchange showing text as the fallback channel when a call isn't possible — very common in everyday Korean life
시간하고 장소는 문자로 보낼게요. 확인해 두세요.
I'll text you the time and place. Keep an eye out.
문자로 marks the sending channel; 확인해 두세요 = 'check and remember it' — a natural pair when sending important details
전화 안 받으시면 문자 보낼게요.
If you don't pick up, I'll text you.
Backup-plan promise using -으시면 ('if you') — shows the two channels working together, as Koreans routinely use both
nuance: 문자 보낼게요 = 'I'll send a text (SMS)'. 문자 is Sino-Korean 文字 ('written characters'), short for 문자 메시지. The important lexical landscape for a Korean learner: 문자 (formal 'SMS text'), 문자 메시지 (full form), 카톡 (KakaoTalk message — what younger Koreans actually use most often), and 메시지 (generic English loanword). In real life 카톡 보낼게요 is extremely common because most personal communication in Korea runs through KakaoTalk, whereas 문자 tends to appear in business, automated verification codes, or when you don't have someone's KakaoTalk. The verb 보내다 ('to send') pairs with the channel particle 로: 문자로 보내다 = 'send BY text'. The ending -ㄹ게요 again signals a first-person promise to the listener, warmer than the bare future -ㄹ 거예요. A subtlety: 보내 줄게요 (adding 주다) adds the nuance of 'I'll send it as a favor for you', slightly more considerate — fine to use but not required. Never mix up 문자 (text) with 전화 (call) in what you promise to send.

structuredNuance.t: 'Written-characters send-will-I' — literally promising to transmit written characters. The real meaning is a commitment to follow up via SMS text message rather than by voice. The 文字 etymology underscores that 문자 is about written script, not a voice channel.

Common on any call when you want to send information (addresses, times, links) that should be written down. The -ㄹ게요 ending is polite-casual — fine for friends, classmates, and colleagues. For clients or formal situations, say 문자 드리겠습니다 or 메시지 보내 드리겠습니다.

문자 = specifically SMS. 카톡 보낼게요 = the default for most personal Korean communication today (KakaoTalk). 메시지 보낼게요 = generic. Never say 전화 보낼게요 — 전화 (call) is placed with 걸다, not sent with 보내다. Mixing these verbs with the wrong nouns is a telltale learner error.

The channel can shift without changing the grammar frame: 문자 보낼게요 (SMS, the formal default) → 카톡 보낼게요 (KakaoTalk, the most common in personal life) → 메시지 보낼게요 (channel-neutral). Adding 주다 gives 문자 보내 줄게요 ('I'll send it as a favor for you'), slightly warmer. The channel particle 로 specifies means: 문자로 보낼게요. For formal or client-facing contexts step up to 문자 드리겠습니다 or 메시지 보내 드리겠습니다.

Mixing up 문자 (text) with 전화 (call) and saying 전화 보낼게요 is wrong — you send (보내다) a 문자 but place (걸다) a 전화. Also, omitting 로 when naming the channel (say 문자로 보낼게요, not just 문자 보낼게요, if specifying the channel matters in context).

mistakes: Mixing up 문자 (a text message) with 전화 (a phone call) and saying 전화 보낼게요 — you send (보내다) a 문자 but place (걸다) a 전화; the verb and noun must match.
Omitting the channel particle 로 when it matters — 문자로 보내다 means 'send by text', while 문자 보내다 without 로 is fine informally but may be ambiguous if other channels are being discussed.
Forgetting -ㄹ게요 is first-person — you can't say 그 사람이 문자 보낼게요; for third-party actions use 보낼 거예요 or 보낸대요.

usage: 메모 남겨 주세요.
Please leave a message.
남기다 = to leave (something) behind; -어 주세요 = polite favor request
성함하고 연락처 남겨 주세요.
Please leave your name and contact number.
Standard office intake: 성함 (honorific 'name') + 연락처 ('contact details') — both objects of 남기다
삐 소리 후에 남겨 주세요.
Please leave it after the beep.
삐 소리 = the beep tone; 후에 = after — the classic voicemail prompt wording
용건 간단히 남겨 주세요.
Please leave a brief message about your business.
용건 = the purpose/matter; 간단히 = briefly — a common voicemail phrase encouraging callers to be concise
examples: A: 이 대리님 계십니까? / B: 지금 자리 비우셨어요. 메모 남겨 주시면 전달해 드릴게요.
A: Is Deputy Manager Lee in? / B: He's stepped away. If you leave a message I'll pass it along.
Typical office reception exchange: checking availability and offering to relay a message — 전달해 드릴게요 is the key follow-up phrase
삐 소리 후에 성함과 메모 남겨 주세요. 연락드리겠습니다.
After the beep, please leave your name and a message. I'll get back to you.
Complete voicemail greeting format: beep cue → name + message request → callback promise
연결이 안 되는 것 같아요. 혹시 메모라도 남겨 드릴까요?
It seems we can't reach them. Shall I at least leave a message for you?
메모라도 = 'even just a message' (라도 signals doing the lesser option); the 드릴까요 offers the service from a service-provider perspective
nuance: 메모 남겨 주세요 = 'please leave a message/note'. 메모 is the English loanword 'memo', used for a brief written or spoken message left for someone who wasn't available. The verb 남기다 'to leave (something) behind' is the crucial choice: English uses a single word 'leave' for both leaving a place (떠나다) and leaving an object behind (남기다), so learners reach for 떠나다 — never correct here. 남기다 is transitive: it takes a direct object (메모를, 이름을, 연락처를), and the politeness is carried by -어 주세요 ('please do X for me/as a favor'). Stripping that down to just 남겨 sounds like a curt command. Close synonyms: 메시지 남겨 주세요 is interchangeable (메시지 = English-derived 'message', slightly more modern), and 전할 말씀 있으세요? ('do you have something you'd like relayed?') is what a secretary proactively asks rather than instructing the caller. In the fine-grained register of Korean office calls: 메모를 남기다 = to leave a written note, while 음성 메시지를 남기다 = to leave a voice message — the modifier distinguishes the two. Collocations: 성함 / 연락처 / 용건을 남기다.

structuredNuance.t: 'Memo leave please' — 남기다 means 'make something remain behind (for someone)'. The real meaning is asking the caller to deposit a note or spoken message so the unavailable person can respond later. The intent is ensuring no communication is lost.

Used by receptionists, recorded voicemails, or secretaries when the intended person is unavailable. The -어 주세요 ending is polite-standard and appropriate in any professional or semi-formal phone setting. For customers or important callers, soften further: 메모 남겨 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or offer 전할 말씀 있으세요?

structuredNuance.e: VS 메시지 남겨 주세요 / 전할 말씀 있으세요?
structuredNuance.t: 메모 남겨 주세요 and 메시지 남겨 주세요 are interchangeable; 메시지 is slightly more modern/informal. 전할 말씀 있으세요? is what you proactively ask (pushing agency to the caller) rather than instructing them to leave something.

The instruction ladder: 메모 남겨 주세요 (standard) ↔ 메시지 남겨 주세요 (same register; 메시지 is slightly more informal and modern). Specify medium: 음성 메시지 남겨 주세요 (voice message). Make it conditional and deferential: 메모 남겨 주시면 전달해 드리겠습니다 (receptionist's full formula). Flip to proactive offer: 전할 말씀 있으세요? (secretary actively asking the caller). Voicemail prompt format: 삐 소리 후에 성함과 용건을 남겨 주세요.

English 'leave a message' uses one verb for both leaving a place and leaving an object. In Korean these are different verbs: 떠나다 = leave a place, 남기다 = leave something behind for someone. Using 떠나다 here (메시지를 떠나세요) is nonsensical — 남기다 is the only correct choice.

mistakes: Reaching for 떠나다 because English says 'leave' — 떠나다 is leaving a PLACE; leaving a note or message behind is 남기다, so it's 메모 남겨 주세요.
Dropping 주세요 and saying just 메모 남겨 — that's a blunt command; the -어 주세요 construction is what makes it a polite favor request.
Calling the message 편지 — 편지 is a postal letter; a phone message is 메모 or 메시지.

usage: 끊지 마세요.
Please don't hang up.
끊다 = to cut/sever (the line); -지 마세요 = polite negative command 'please don't ~'
잠깐만요, 끊지 마세요.
One sec, please don't hang up.
잠깐만요 is the verbal gesture that freezes the moment — followed by 끊지 마세요 to keep the other person on the line
아직 끊지 마세요.
Don't hang up yet.
아직 = 'not yet' — signals more is coming and asks them to hold on a little longer
바로 바꿔 드릴 테니 끊지 마세요.
I'll transfer you right away, so don't hang up.
-ㄹ 테니 links a promised action to the request — natural in reception or call-centre speech
examples: A: 잠깐만요! 끊지 마세요. 담당자 확인해 볼게요. / B: 네, 알겠어요.
A: One moment! Don't hang up. Let me check with the person in charge. / B: Okay, understood.
Classic call-centre hold request: the agent asks the caller to wait; the caller's 네, 알겠어요 confirms they'll stay on
끊지 마세요, 잠깐 바꿔 드릴게요.
Don't hang up, I'll put you through in a sec.
Collocating with 바꿔 드릴게요 — the standard pair for transferring a call
아직 할 얘기가 있어요. 끊지 마세요.
I still have something to say. Don't hang up.
Used in a personal call when the other person is about to end it too soon — 아직 (not yet) sets up the reason
nuance: 끊지 마세요 = 'please don't hang up'. The verb 끊다 means 'to cut or sever', which is exactly how Koreans conceptualise ending a phone call — you 'cut' the connection, the natural opposite of 걸다 ('hook' a call). This cut metaphor extends: 담배를 끊다 ('quit smoking'), 연락을 끊다 ('cut off contact'), 말을 끊다 ('interrupt someone's speech'). Context makes it clear which 끊다 is in play. The grammar core is -지 말다 → -지 마세요 ('please don't V'): attach -지 마세요 directly to the dictionary stem (끊 + 지 마세요). The error English speakers make is using 안 instead: 안 끊어요 simply describes your own action ('I'm not hanging up') — it has NO power to instruct the other person to stop. Prohibitions need -지 마세요. Politeness levels: 끊지 마 (반말, close friends only), 끊지 마세요 (standard polite), 끊지 마십시오 (formal announcements). The phrase collocates most naturally with 잠깐만요 and 바꿔 드릴게요, the two phrases most often said right before asking someone to hold.

structuredNuance.t: 'Cut-don't please' — 끊다 literally means to cut or sever. On a phone call it means severing the connection (hanging up). The metaphor is vivid: you hooked (걸다) the call and now you're severing (끊다) it. 끊지 마세요 asks the other person not to sever that connection.

Mostly heard in call-centre or office settings when you need the caller to wait for a transfer, or in personal calls when you need a moment. The 마세요 ending is polite and works universally. In formal recorded announcements: 끊지 마십시오. With close friends: 끊지 마. Always pair with a reason or action: 잠깐만요, 확인할게요, 바꿔 드릴게요.

잠깐 기다리세요 ('please wait a moment') and 끊지 마세요 ('please don't hang up') often appear together. The difference: 기다리세요 focuses on the waiting; 끊지 마세요 specifically warns against ending the call. In practice both appear back to back: 잠깐 기다리세요, 끊지 마세요.

Register ladder: 끊지 마 (반말, close friends only — casual but not rude in the right relationship) → 끊지 마세요 (standard polite, the everyday default with strangers and colleagues) → 끊지 마십시오 (formal / recorded announcement register). The verb 끊다 carries the same meaning across all these levels. Related uses of 끊다 beyond phone calls: 담배를 끊다 (quit smoking), 연락을 끊다 (cut off contact), 말을 끊다 (interrupt speech) — context always disambiguates.

Saying 안 끊어요 to mean 'don't hang up' only describes your own present action ('I'm not hanging up') — it cannot command someone else. Prohibitions in Korean require -지 마세요, not 안. Also: 끄지 마세요 is wrong here (끄다 = turn off a device); ending a call is 끊다.

mistakes: Saying 안 끊어요 to mean 'don't hang up' — that only states your own current action; a prohibition directed at another person needs -지 마세요, i.e. 끊지 마세요.
Using 끄다 instead of 끊다 — 끄다 is 'to turn off (a device or light)'; ending a call is 끊다 ('to cut the line'), so 'don't hang up' is 끊지 마세요, not 끄지 마세요.
Clipping to 끊지 마 with someone you owe politeness — the 세요 is needed for anyone other than a close friend.

usage: 잠깐 기다리세요.
Please wait a moment.
잠깐 = briefly (spoken); 기다리다 = to wait; -세요 = polite request
잠깐만 기다리세요.
Just one moment, please.
잠깐만 (with 만 'only/just') feels a shade shorter and more urgent — 'just this one brief moment'
잠깐 기다려 주세요.
Please wait a moment (for me).
-어 주세요 adds a favor framing — sounds warmer and more considerate; preferred for customers
여기서 잠깐 기다리세요.
Please wait here a moment.
여기서 marks the location the person should stay — used in person when directing someone to a waiting spot
examples: A: 박 부장님 좀 바꿔 주시겠어요? / B: 잠깐 기다려 주세요. 지금 바로 연결해 드릴게요.
A: Could you put Manager Park on? / B: Please hold a moment. I'll connect you right now.
Call-transfer sequence: request → hold instruction + callback promise; 기다려 주세요 here instead of 기다리세요 because the caller is a customer who deserves the favor framing
잠깐만 기다리세요. 메모지 좀 찾을게요.
Just a moment please. Let me find some notepaper.
잠깐만 signals you'll be extremely quick; explaining WHY you're pausing (메모지 찾을게요) is courteous Korean phone etiquette
네, 잠깐만요. 담당자 바로 바꿔 드리겠습니다.
Yes, just one moment. I'll put the person in charge on right away.
잠깐만요 as a standalone exclamation to freeze the moment, then the promise — a very natural call-centre or office formula
nuance: 잠깐 기다리세요 = 'please wait a moment' — 잠깐 is the everyday spoken adverb for a brief pause, while its near-twin 잠시 carries the same meaning but skews slightly more formal or written (잠시만 기다려 주십시오 is the announcement register heard at service counters). The verb 기다리다 'to wait' is entirely regular here. The crucial register distinction is between 잠깐 기다리세요 (a polite command, -세요) and 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (-어 주세요 = please do it as a favor for me): the 주세요 version is warmer and is strongly preferred in customer-facing situations. A complementary phrase 잠깐만요 ('just a second!') is often thrown out first as a verbal gesture to freeze the conversation, then followed by 기다리세요 or 기다려 주세요. The English-speaker trap is calquing 'hold on' as 잡으세요 (잡다 = physically grab) — that phrase is not used for phone holding; always 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Don't confuse 기다리다 ('wait') with 기대하다 ('expect / look forward to') — similar syllables, completely different meanings.

structuredNuance.t: Literally 'briefly wait-please' — 잠깐 (briefly) + 기다리다 (to wait) + -세요 (polite command). The real function is asking someone to pause in place while you do something — finding a person to transfer to, checking information, or fetching a note. The brevity adverb 잠깐 implicitly promises you won't take long.

The -세요 form is polite and works in most settings. In customer service, service counters, or when the other person is your social superior, prefer 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (favor framing) or the fully formal 잠시만 기다려 주십시오. With close friends: 잠깐 기다려 or 잠깐만. The standalone 잠깐만요 is used as a conversational freeze before the full instruction.

잠시만 기다려 주세요 is the formal near-synonym: 잠시 (잠깐's more formal twin) + 만 (limiting particle 'just') + 기다려 주세요 (favor request). The difference is purely register — 잠시 belongs in service announcements, formal business calls, and written Korean, while 잠깐 is the natural everyday spoken choice. In customer-facing calls 잠시만 기다려 주세요 or 잠시만요 signals extra deference.

The register ladder from casual to formal: 잠깐만 (반말-level shortcut, friends) → 잠깐만요 (standalone freeze exclamation, all contexts) → 잠깐 기다리세요 (polite command) → 잠깐 기다려 주세요 (warmer; favor framing with 주세요) → 잠시만 기다려 주세요 (formal; 잠시 is more written/announcement) → 잠시만 기다려 주십시오 (most formal; service counter / recorded announcement register). Each step up adds one layer of deference.

Translating 'hold on' as 잡으세요 is wrong — 잡다 means to physically grip something; for phone-hold always use 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요. Also, confusing 기다리다 (wait) with 기대하다 (expect/look forward to): they share syllables but mean completely different things.

mistakes: Translating 'hold on' as 잡으세요 — 잡다 means to physically grab; 'please wait/hold' on a phone call is 잠깐 기다리세요 or 끊지 마세요.
Confusing 기다리다 (wait) with 기대하다 (expect/look forward to) — they share an opening syllable but are completely different; 'please wait' is only 기다리세요.
Using the bare command 잠깐 기다려 with a customer or elder — for respectful contexts always add -세요 or use the fuller 잠깐 기다려 주세요.

usage: 연락해 주세요.
Please get in touch.
연락하다 = to make contact (by any channel — call, text, email, messenger)
도착하면 연락해 주세요.
Please contact me when you arrive.
-(으)면 sets the trigger condition — 'once X happens, do Y'
꼭 연락해 주세요.
Please be sure to reach out.
꼭 = 'without fail, definitely' — adds urgency to the request
편하실 때 연락해 주세요.
Please contact me whenever's convenient for you.
편하실 때 ('when it is comfortable/convenient for you') is deferential and leaves timing entirely to the other person
examples: A: 그럼 오늘 결정 나면 연락해 주세요. / B: 네, 알겠습니다. 바로 연락 드릴게요.
A: Then please contact me once you decide today. / B: Yes, understood. I'll reach out right away.
Business exchange: A requests contact on a condition; B promises it with the humble 연락 드릴게요 — shows both sides of the phrase in a real professional context
문제 생기면 언제든지 연락해 주세요.
If any problem comes up, reach out any time.
언제든지 ('any time') combined with the condition -면 makes this a standing open invitation — very common at the end of a service call
결정하시면 저한테 연락해 주세요. 다른 분한테 말씀하시면 제가 못 받을 수도 있어요.
Once you've decided, please contact me directly. If you tell someone else I might not receive it.
저한테 marks 'to me' as the specific destination — the contrast 저한테 vs 다른 분한테 teaches the 한테 particle direction naturally
nuance: 연락해 주세요 = 'please contact me'. 연락 is Sino-Korean 連絡 (連 link + 絡 tie/entwine), literally 'making a link' — and critically, it is channel-agnostic: it covers phone calls, texts, emails, KakaoTalk, or any other means of reaching someone. Use 연락하다 when you don't care how they reach you; reach for 전화하다 only if you specifically want a voice call. Structurally, 연락해 주세요 = 연락해 (연락하다 contracted) + 주세요 (favor request). The destination particle is 한테/에게, not 를: 저한테 연락해 주세요 ('contact me'); saying 저를 연락하다 is ungrammatical. A very common shortened form is 연락 주세요 (dropping 하), which natives use constantly with no change in meaning. For formal or client-facing contexts, step up to 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 or the humble 연락드리겠습니다 (when YOU are the one promising to reach out). Don't conflate 연락 with 약속 ('a promised appointment'): 연락 is merely reaching out; 약속 commits to an actual meeting time.

structuredNuance.t: 'Link-make please-do-for-me' — 連絡 (연락) literally means 'making a link/tie'. The real meaning is any act of reaching out — a call, text, email, or message — to let someone know something. Its channel-agnostic breadth is the defining feature.
chips: 連絡 (연락) = link/tie → contact by any channel

structuredNuance.t: The -아/어 주세요 form is polite and standard for peers, colleagues, and most situations. For clients, customers, or seniors, upgrade: 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (deferential) or 연락 부탁드립니다 (formal). The short form 연락 주세요 is extremely common in casual and semi-formal speech.

전화해 주세요 specifically requests a voice call and nothing else — you are limiting the channel. 연락해 주세요 covers any channel — call, text, KakaoTalk, email — and is the right phrase whenever you don't want to restrict how the other person reaches you. In casual speech 연락 줘 (반말) is the clipped form; 전화 줘 specifically demands a call.

The register and formality ladder: 연락 줘 (반말, close friends) → 연락해 주세요 (polite-casual, everyday default) → 연락 주세요 (clipped but equally polite; omitting 하 is natural) → 연락 부탁드립니다 (formal, written-style) → 연락 주시면 감사하겠습니다 (maximally deferential, client or senior). When YOU are the one promising: 연락할게요 (casual-polite commitment) or 연락드리겠습니다 (humble, formal).

Marking the person with 를: 저를 연락해 주세요 is ungrammatical — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 as the direction marker. Also, using 전화해 주세요 when you mean any channel — 전화하다 is specifically a phone call; for open-channel contact always use 연락하다.

mistakes: Marking the person with 를: 저를 연락해 주세요 is wrong — 연락하다 takes 한테/에게 as the direction, so it's 저한테 연락해 주세요.
Using 전화해 주세요 when you mean any channel — 전화하다 is specifically a voice call; for 'reach out however you like', 연락해 주세요 is the correct phrase.
Forgetting it's a 하다-verb: the polite present is 연락해요 (not 연락하어요), the request is 연락해 주세요, and the humble promise is 연락드리겠습니다.

usage: 김민수 씨 바꿔 주세요.
Please put Kim Minsu on.
[name] 바꿔 주세요 = ask for that specific person — the standard way to request someone on a call
담당자 좀 바꿔 주세요.
Could you put the person in charge on?
좀 ('a bit') softens the request — essential politeness when you don't know the person's name
과장님 계시면 바꿔 주세요.
If the manager's there, please put him on.
계시면 = 'if (he/she) is in' — the honorific conditional; saves face if the person turns out to be away
내선 203번 바꿔 주세요.
Please connect me to extension 203.
내선 번호 = extension number; 바꿔 주세요 works equally for persons and extension numbers
examples: A: 여보세요, 영업부 이 과장님 바꿔 주세요. / B: 잠깐만요, 연결해 드리겠습니다.
A: Hello, please put Deputy Manager Lee from the sales department on. / B: One moment, I'll connect you.
Complete office call formula: department + name + title + 바꿔 주세요, followed by the receptionist's hold-and-transfer response
엄마 집에 계시면 좀 바꿔 주세요.
If mom's home, could you put her on?
Calling the family landline: 좀 softens what would otherwise sound like a demand; 계시면 adds the polite conditional
죄송하지만 책임자분 바꿔 주시겠어요?
I'm sorry, but could you put the person in charge on?
죄송하지만 prefaces a potentially demanding request; -주시겠어요? (would you please?) is the softest, most deferential form — right for a complaint call or when talking to a senior
nuance: 바꿔 주세요 on the phone means 'please switch who is speaking / put ___ on'. The verb 바꾸다 'to change, switch, swap' is the same word used for exchanging goods (돈을 바꾸다 'exchange money') or changing clothes, and that overlap is the learner's trap: on a phone call, 바꿔 주세요 isn't asking to trade anything physical — it's asking the person who answered to hand the line to someone else. Think of it as 'swap the speaker'. The form: 바꾸 + 어 주세요 → 바꿔 주세요 (ㅜ+어 contracts to 워). The pattern is [person or extension] + 바꿔 주세요. Near-synonym: 연결해 주세요 ('please connect me') is what you say to an automated switchboard or in formal writing; 바꿔 주세요 is what you say when a live human answered and you need a different person. For extra deference: 바꿔 주시겠어요? ('would you please put them on?'). Never calque English 'put on' as 놓다 or 올리다 — those verbs have no phone-transfer function in Korean.

structuredNuance.t: 'Change/swap please-do-for-me' — 바꾸다 means to swap or exchange. On a call the real meaning is 'swap who is speaking': hand the phone to ___ or transfer the line to that person. No physical object is being exchanged; the 'thing' being switched is the active speaker.

Use when a live person has answered and you need someone else. The pattern is [name/title/extension] + 바꿔 주세요. Add 좀 for softness, 죄송하지만 when you're making a demanding request, and -주시겠어요? for maximum deference. With automated systems, 연결해 주세요 is more natural. In formal business, announce your own name first before making the request.

연결해 주세요 ('please connect me') is the near-synonym; it emphasizes the technical connection and is the standard phrasing with automated systems, switchboards, or in written Korean. 바꿔 주세요 is the natural spoken form when a person answers and you want a different human on the line.

The softness ladder: 바꿔 주세요 (standard polite, everyday default) → 좀 바꿔 주세요 (softer; 좀 acts as a polite buffer) → 바꿔 주시겠어요? (deferential request; -겠어요 makes it a question, more indirect and respectful — use with seniors or on a complaint call). Formal alternative: 연결해 주세요 (emphasises the technical transfer; preferred with switchboards or automated systems). Check availability first: 계시면 바꿔 주세요 (conditional form, saves face if they're out).

The verb 바꾸다 also means 'exchange goods', so learners misread 바꿔 주세요 as a physical trade on a call — it isn't. Also, calquing 'put on' as 놓다 or 올리다 doesn't work in Korean; the only phrase for phone transfer is 바꿔 주세요 or 연결해 주세요.

mistakes: Reading 바꿔 주세요 as 'exchange something' on a call — here 바꾸다 means swap who is on the line; [name] 바꿔 주세요 = 'please put that person on', no goods involved.
Calquing English 'put on' with 놓다 or 올리다 — neither verb means phone transfer; the set phrase is [person/extension] + 바꿔 주세요.
Mis-contracting the vowel: the correct form is 바꿔 (from 바꾸+어), not 바껴 주세요 — 바꿔 is sometimes written in full as 바꾸어 주세요 in formal script but always contracted to 바꿔 in speech.

usage: 전화 잘못 걸었어요.
I dialed the wrong number.
잘못 = adverb 'wrongly/mistakenly'; 걸었어요 = past tense of 걸다 (place a call)
죄송해요, 전화 잘못 걸었어요.
Sorry, wrong number.
Apology-first is the Korean social reflex — lead with 죄송해요 before explaining, then hang up politely with 끊을게요
제가 번호를 잘못 눌렀어요.
I pressed the wrong digit.
누르다 = 'to press'; 잘못 눌렀어요 = pressed wrongly — an alternative natural phrasing, especially after mistyping on a touchscreen
전화 잘못 거셨어요.
You've reached the wrong number.
거셨어요 = honorific past of 걸다 — what YOU say when the CALLER has dialled wrong; honorific even to the unknown caller
examples: A: 여보세요, 거기 이삿짐 센터죠? / B: 아니요, 전화 잘못 걸었어요. / A: 아, 죄송합니다.
A: Hello, is that the moving company? / B: No, you've got the wrong number. / A: Oh, I'm so sorry.
Real A/B exchange showing both sides: the caller's mistaken assumption and the natural polite correction — 죄송합니다 from the caller is the expected follow-up
아, 전화 잘못 걸었어요. 죄송해요. 끊을게요.
Oh, wrong number. Sorry. I'll hang up.
The three-part Korean wrong-number etiquette: realize → apologize → announce hang-up; saying 끊을게요 before dropping is polite, not optional
번호를 잘못 봐서 전화 잘못 걸었어요. 정말 죄송합니다.
I misread the number and dialed wrong. I'm truly sorry.
Explaining the cause (잘못 보다 = misread) alongside the admission — 정말 죄송합니다 is a more emphatic apology, used when you've caused extra inconvenience
nuance: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I called the wrong number'. The spine is 잘못, which operates here as an ADVERB meaning 'wrongly, by mistake', and must be written as a separate word from the verb (잘못 걸었어요, not 잘못걸었어요). Learners trip over two different 잘못: the adverb (잘못 하다 = 'do wrongly') and the noun (잘못 = 'a fault/mistake', as in 제 잘못이에요 'it's my fault'). In this phrase it is the adverb. The second pitfall is 잘못 vs 못: 못 걸었어요 = 'I couldn't place the call' (inability), while 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I placed it wrongly (wrong number)' — one syllable apart, entirely different meaning. Korean phone etiquette expects a three-step wrong-number exit: (1) 죄송해요 or 죄송합니다 (apologize), (2) 전화 잘못 걸었어요 (explain), (3) 끊을게요 or 실례할게요 (announce the hang-up and go). Silently disconnecting skips steps 1–3 and is considered rude. When YOU receive a wrong-number call, you politely tell the caller 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific past), honoring them even in their error.

structuredNuance.t: 'Phone wrongly-hooked-did' — 잘못 (wrongly) + 걸다 (hook/place a call) + past tense. The literal hook-a-call metaphor is the same one in 전화를 걸다 ('place a call'). The real meaning is 'I placed this call by mistake to the wrong number'.

Say it the instant you realize you've dialled wrong — before asking questions, always apologize first (죄송해요), state the reason briefly (전화 잘못 걸었어요), then signal you're hanging up (끊을게요). The 요-ending is polite and universal for strangers. With close friends, 잘못 걸었어 (반말) is fine.

번호가 틀렸어요 ('the number is wrong') is what you say about the number itself — e.g. when confirming someone gave you bad information. 잘못 눌렀어요 ('I pressed the wrong key') focuses on the physical dialling error, natural for touchscreen mis-taps. 전화 잘못 걸었어요 is the broadest and most common form.

Your own admission: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 (polite, the standard) → 잘못 걸었어 (반말, close friends only). Telling the caller they dialled wrong: 전화 잘못 거셨어요 (honorific past -셨어요, shows respect even to a stranger who called in error). Naming the cause: 번호를 잘못 봐서요 (misread the number) or 잘못 눌렀어요 (pressed a wrong digit — most natural for touchscreen callers). The full three-step exit formula is: 죄송해요, 전화 잘못 걸었어요, 끊을게요.

Confusing the adverb 잘못 ('wrongly') with 못 ('couldn't'): 못 걸었어요 = 'I couldn't call' (inability), 잘못 걸었어요 = 'I called wrongly' (wrong number). Also, treating 잘못 as the noun 'fault' and trying to conjugate it: as an adverb it never inflects, always stays 잘못 as a separate word before the verb.

mistakes: Confusing 잘못 (adverb 'mistakenly') with 못 — 못 걸었어요 means 'I couldn't call' (inability); the wrong-number admission uses the adverb 잘못: 전화 잘못 걸었어요 ('called wrongly').
Fusing 잘못 to the verb: 잘못걸었어요 (no space) looks like a compound and is a spelling error — keep them separate: 전화 잘못 걸었어요.
Hanging up silently without speaking — Korean phone etiquette requires 죄송해요, 전화 잘못 걸었어요, and 끊을게요 before you go; silent disconnection is considered rude.
